stanzas: “Oh, full, full is my little box,
Come out, come out into the tall rye!
There I will wait until nightfall,
And when I catch sight of the dark-eyed one —
I will lay out all my wares.
I paid no small prices myself.
Do not haggle, do not be stingy:
Come, hold up your scarlet lips,
Sit closer to your dear one!”
And now the misty night has fallen,
Hark, she comes! — the longed-for one has come,
She keeps fearing to pay too much.
The lad and the girl kiss,
He asks her to raise the price.

notes: IMPORT: orig lines 1.8 and 2.6 begin with Wikisource's verse numbers ('20 Все товары разложу.', '30 Всё боится передать.'): strip them from orig; en and rom leave them out.
line 1.1: 'коробушка' is a diminutive of 'короб', the pedlar's box or pack carried on the back (the korobeiniki are the pedlars who carry it).
line 1.3-1.4: 'take pity on a young fellow's shoulder' means: buy something and lighten the load he carries.
line 1.5: 'Выди' is a folk/poetic form of 'выйди' (come out).
line 2.6: 'передать' here means to overpay, to give more than the thing is worth.
line 2.7: 'цалуется' is the older spelling of 'целуется' (kisses); romanized as written.
line 2.8: 'asks her to raise the price' plays on the bargaining: he asks for more in return (more kisses). The subject is the lad.
line 1.3: 'зазнобушка', an affectionate folk word for a sweetheart (from 'зазноба').
